title: Writing Your First Method
description: Give a block of code a name so you can run it whenever you like.

items: Every program so far lived inside `public static void main(String[] args)`. That is a **method**.
A method is a named block of instructions.
Write it once. Run it whenever you like by writing its name and `()`. That is called **calling** the method.
content.title: A method

content.text: A recipe keeps its steps in one place, under one name. You follow it whenever you need it. A method does the same for lines of code.

content.caption: The three banner lines are written once and printed twice. Change the banner and both copies change, because there is only one copy.

content.question: What is the main reason to write a method?
options: To make the program run faster
Write steps once, then reuse them by name
To repeat a line for ever
content.explain: A method keeps a group of steps in one place under one name. You call the name instead of copying lines, and a fix only needs one edit.

parts.label: modifier
parts.note: Every method that sits beside `main` needs it. Module 8 explains what it means.

parts.label: return type
parts.note: `void` means the method hands nothing back.

parts.label: name
parts.note: lowerCamelCase, like a variable. It should read as an instruction.

parts.label: parameters
parts.note: Empty brackets: the method needs nothing from the caller.

content.title: Anatomy of a method header
content.caption: Every method you write in the next two modules has this shape.

items.sub: `printBanner`, `drawLine`, `askAge`. If you cannot name it in two or three words, it does too many jobs.
Methods sit side by side with `main`, never inside it.
Java reads the whole class before it runs anything.

content.caption: `sayHello` and `drawLine` are written below `main`, and the calls still work.

content.question: Which line correctly starts a method named `wave`?
content.explain: You need the modifier `static`, the return type `void`, the name, and the brackets: `static void wave() {`.

content.value: A call is a detour. Java leaves the line it is on, runs the whole method, then comes back to exactly where it left off.

steps.note: A call. Java leaves `main` and jumps into `step`.
The method ran out of lines, so Java returns to `main`, just after the call.

content.title: Watch Java jump in and back
content.outro: Nothing is skipped and nothing runs twice. If you can trace these four lines, you understand method calls.

content.caption: A method can call another method. Here `main` calls `printReport`, which calls `drawLine` twice.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: Java jumps into `hi` at the call, prints `B`, then comes back and carries on with `C`.

items.sub: `printBanner()` says what is about to happen. Three `println` lines full of `=` do not.
Repeated code has to be fixed in every copy, and one copy always gets missed.
When `main` is a list of calls, you can read the whole program's shape on one screen.

items.title: Copied
items.text: The same four lines, written twice.

items.title: With a method
items.text: The loop lives in one place, under a name.

content.title: Same output, two ways
content.caption: Same output, and `main` now says **what** it does. But `printThreeStars` is stuck on three. Telling a method what to work with is the next lesson. Tip: if a method needs a comment, try a better name first.

content.question: How many times does this print `***`?
content.explain: Each call runs the whole method body again, and there are three calls.

items.title: Missing brackets
items.text: `error: not a statement`. Without `()`, Java sees a name, not a call. Fix: `printBanner();`

items.title: Method inside main
items.text: `error: illegal start of expression`. Fix: close `main` with `}` first, then write the method below it.

content.title: Both of these fail to compile
content.caption: The brackets are what make a call a call, even when there is nothing inside them. Methods are siblings of `main`, never children of it.

content.value: One misplaced method can produce three errors or more. Fix the **first** error and compile again: the rest are usually echoes of it.
content.title: Fix the first error first

content.question: What does javac say about the line `printBanner;`?
options: It compiles and prints the banner
content.explain: Without brackets it is not a call, just a name on its own, and a name on its own is not an instruction.

practice.question: Write a method called printGoodbye that prints two lines, then call it twice from main.
Write drawLine so that it prints 20 dashes using a loop, then call it above and below a title in main.
This does not compile because the method is inside main. Move one brace to fix it.
Write a method runAll that calls drawLine, then sayHello, then drawLine. main should call only runAll.

quiz.question: What is a method?
options: A named block of instructions you can run by calling its name
A variable that holds several values
quiz.explain: `main` is one too. Naming a block lets you run it from anywhere, as often as you like.

quiz.question: Where do your own methods go?
options: Inside the class, beside main but not inside it
quiz.explain: Methods are siblings of `main`. A method declared inside `main` gives `illegal start of expression`.

quiz.question: What does `void` mean in `static void printBanner()`?
options: The method hands nothing back to whoever called it
The method takes no values in
quiz.explain: `void` is the return type. The empty brackets are what say it takes nothing in.

quiz.question: What happens after a called method finishes?
options: The program carries on at the line right after the call
quiz.explain: A call is a detour, not a jump. Java always comes back to where it left off.

quiz.question: Why does `printBanner;` fail to compile?
options: Without brackets it is not a call, and a bare name is not an instruction
It needs the word static in front of it
quiz.explain: The error is `not a statement`. The round brackets are what make a call, even when there is nothing to put in them.
